title: The year the sea stars melted
teaches: Sea star wasting and the urchins that followed

blocks.text: In June 2013 biologists surveying tide pools on the Olympic coast of Washington found ochre stars with white sores. By late summer divers in Howe Sound, near Vancouver, were finding sunflower stars in the same state. These are big, soft sea stars, as wide as a car tyre, with up to twenty-four arms, the fastest sea stars there are, gliding a metre a minute across the seafloor on thousands of tube feet, the small suckered tubes under each arm. The sick ones twisted, their arms fell off and crawled away on their own, and the bodies dissolved into a white mush on the bottom. Within months it was being reported along the whole coast.

Over the next two years the disease, called **sea star wasting**, struck more than twenty species of sea star from Mexico to Alaska. On the shore it killed most of the ochre stars, the purple and orange stars of Robert Paine's experiment in lesson 7. On the seafloor it was worse. The sunflower star, once common from Baja California to the Aleutians, fell by more than 90 percent across its range, and in the warmer south it disappeared altogether. In 2020 it was listed as critically endangered.

blocks.caption: A sunflower star, a fast seafloor hunter with up to twenty-four arms.

blocks.text: Lesson 7 called the ochre star a keystone, a species whose loss changes much more than its own numbers. It showed what happens on the shore when it goes: mussels spread down into the space it kept open, and the shore holds fewer kinds. After 2014, on some shores, that began to happen. But young ochre stars arrived in large numbers within a couple of years, and on many shores they grew back before the mussels took over.

The sunflower star's loss had nothing to make up for it. It eats sea urchins, and urchins eat kelp. Lesson 8's chain of otter, urchin and kelp has a second top predator in it, and in the waters where otters were absent, including most of the coast south of Washington, the sunflower star was the one keeping urchins down. When it vanished, purple urchins multiplied, came out of the crevices where they had hidden from it, and began to eat the kelp forests.

blocks.caption: A shore patch and a stretch of seafloor from 2010. Ochre stars eat mussels; sunflower stars eat urchins; urchins eat kelp. Choose which stars survive the wasting of 2013, and whether the sea warms. A model.
blocks.task: Guess, then take away the sunflower stars

blocks.text: In northern California the timing could not have been worse. From 2014 to 2016 a patch of unusually warm water, nicknamed the Blob, spread along the coast. Kelp grows poorly in warm water low in nutrients, so the forests were already thinning when the urchins came. Between them, the warm water and the urchins cut the bull kelp forests off northern California by more than 90 percent, and the red abalone that lived on the kelp starved[^abalone].

Where the kelp was gone, the seafloor became an **urchin barren**: bare rock covered with purple urchins, which can survive for years on almost nothing, with their roe shrunk to nothing, so they are not even worth harvesting. A barren can last long after its cause is gone, since the urchins eat any young kelp that settles. Divers in some places now smash or collect urchins by hand to clear patches where kelp can come back[^urchins].

Finding what kills wild animals is hard. The classic test, set out by the German doctor Robert Koch in the 1880s[^koch], is to find a germ in every sick animal, grow it on its own, give it to healthy animals, and watch them fall ill. Each step is difficult in the sea, where animals can't easily be kept and the water carries countless microbes.

In 2014 researchers reported a virus in sick stars, but later work found it in healthy ones too, and the idea faded. Warm water seemed to make the disease worse, but it struck in cold water as well. Then in 2025, after four years of experiments, a team led by Alyssa Gehman and Melanie Prentice at the Hakai Institute and the University of British Columbia reported that a bacterium, *Vibrio pectenicida*, caused the wasting. They grew it from the fluid of sick sunflower stars, gave it to healthy ones raised in clean seawater, and the healthy stars wasted and died.

Knowing the cause opens the way to protecting the stars that are left and to bringing them back. At the University of Washington's Friday Harbor Laboratories in the San Juan Islands, biologists learned to raise sunflower stars from eggs in tanks, and the first young stars have been returned to the sea in trials[^friday].

blocks.caption: Five questions on the wasting
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Which sea star was hit hardest by the wasting?
choices: The sunflower star, down by more than 90 percent
The ochre star, down by about half
Small sea stars of the high shore
items.why: Ochre stars died in large numbers but young ones refilled many shores within a few years. Sunflower stars have not recovered.

items.ask: Why did losing sunflower stars harm kelp forests?
choices: Sunflower stars ate the urchins that eat kelp
The dead stars poisoned the water
items.why: With their predator gone, urchins multiplied and grazed the kelp, as in lesson 8's chain.

items.ask: What else cut northern California's kelp from 2014 to 2016?
choices: A long spell of warm water poor in nutrients
A rise in the number of sea otters
items.why: The warm-water Blob thinned the kelp just as the urchins came.

items.ask: Why can an urchin barren last after its cause is gone?
choices: Urchins survive on little and eat any young kelp that settles
Kelp can't grow on rock once urchins have been there
Barrens are too deep for kelp
items.why: Starved urchins hang on for years, grazing down each new kelp plant.

items.ask: What finally showed that Vibrio pectenicida caused the wasting?
choices: Healthy stars given the cultured bacterium wasted and died
It was found in the water near sick stars
It appeared in the same years as the warm water
items.why: Growing the germ and giving it to healthy animals is Koch's test of cause, beyond finding it nearby.

summary: **Sea stars began dissolving along the Pacific coast in 2013.** More than twenty species were struck, from Mexico to Alaska.
**The sunflower star fell by over 90 percent.** It was listed as critically endangered in 2020.
**Ochre stars came back faster.** Young stars refilled many shores within a few years.
**Without sunflower stars, urchins ate the kelp.** Lesson 8's chain with a second top predator.
**Warm water hurt the kelp too.** Northern California lost more than 90 percent of its bull kelp, leaving urchin barrens.
**In 2025 a bacterium was named as the cause.** Healthy stars given Vibrio pectenicida wasted, passing Koch's test.

abalone.title: The abalone
abalone.text: Red abalone, big sea snails that graze kelp, had supported a popular dive fishery in northern California. After the kelp died, many starved, and the state closed the fishery in 2018.

urchins.title: Hiding urchins
urchins.text: In a healthy kelp forest urchins mostly stay in crevices and eat drifting pieces of kelp. When predators are few and drift kelp runs short, they come out into the open and graze standing kelp, so a forest can flip to a barren quickly.

friday.title: Raising sunflower stars
friday.text: A sunflower star larva drifts for weeks, then settles as a star smaller than a grain of rice with five arms. It adds arms as it grows, and once it starts eating small clams and mussels it grows quickly.

koch.title: Koch's test
koch.text: Robert Koch used these steps to show which bacteria cause anthrax and tuberculosis. They are called Koch's postulates. They can't always be met, since some germs can't be grown alone, but when they are met they are strong evidence.
